overview.title: Local generalization and its limits
overview.main_topic: Why deep nets achieve only local generalization (to known unknowns, via interpolation on a learned manifold), illustrated by Figure 19.6 and the rocket and city-navigation examples.
overview.central_idea: Deep networks generalize only to inputs close to their training data, because they interpolate on a learned manifold. They therefore need dense sampling of the input space, while humans use abstract models to solve new problems in one or a few trials.
overview.importance: This page ties the chapter's philosophical argument back to the technical account of generalization in chapter 5. It explains in mechanistic terms why deep nets need so much data, why data augmentation works, and why models break under distribution shift.
learning_objectives: Explain why interpolation on a manifold limits deep nets to local generalization.
Explain why data augmentation helps deep nets, in terms of covering factors of variation.
Interpret Figure 19.6 in terms of operational area and information conversion ratio.
Contrast the data requirements of a deep net and a human in the rocket-launch and city-navigation examples.
prerequisites: p.597: automatons vs. intelligent agents and the definition of extreme generalization.
Chapter 5: the manifold hypothesis, interpolation, and dense sampling (pp.169–172).
Chapter 8: the dogs-vs-cats convnet and data augmentation (pp.265, 276).

summary:
The page completes p.597's sentence: deep nets 'can successfully process inputs that deviate a bit from what they're familiar with, which is precisely what makes them useful.' The chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model classified unseen pet photos, as long as they were **close enough** to the training data.

The author names this **local generalization** (Figure 19.6): a deep net's input-to-output mapping 'quickly stops making sense as inputs start deviating from what the net saw at training time.' Deep nets generalize only to **known unknowns**, factors of variation that were anticipated during development and well represented in the training data, such as camera angle or lighting. The cause is that deep nets **generalize via interpolation on a manifold** (chapter 5): every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold. This is why **data augmentation** helps: it fills in factors of variation the data would otherwise lack. Unlike humans, the models cannot improvise when little or no data is available.

**Figure 19.6** shows a 'situations space' with three known situations (dots). A lower-intelligence system turns them into a small **operational area** (small discs around each dot), which is a *lower information conversion ratio*. A higher-intelligence system turns the same three situations into a much larger area, a *higher information conversion ratio*. This anticipates the efficiency-based definition of intelligence on p.604.

Two examples follow. **Rocket to the moon:** a deep net trained by supervised or reinforcement learning would need tens of thousands to millions of launch trials, a **dense sampling** of the input space. Humans use abstraction to build physical models (rocket science) and derive an exact solution in one or a few trials. **City navigation:** a deep net controlling a body would have to 'die many thousands of times' to infer that cars are dangerous, and would have to relearn most of it in a new city. Humans, as p.599 finishes, learn safe behavior without dying once.

paragraphs.excerpt: inputs that deviate a bit from what they’re familiar with, which is precisely
paragraphs.what_it_says: Deep nets can handle inputs that deviate a bit from what they know, which is what makes them useful. The chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model classified new pictures as long as they were close to its training data. But deep nets are limited to local generalization (Figure 19.6): their mapping stops making sense quickly as inputs move away from the training data. They generalize only to known unknowns, factors of variation anticipated during development and heavily featured in the training data (camera angles, lighting). This is because deep nets generalize via interpolation on a manifold (chapter 5), so every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold. That is why basic data augmentation helps so much. Unlike humans, these models cannot improvise when little or no data is available.
paragraphs.what_it_means: **Local generalization** means the model is reliable in a neighborhood of its training samples on the data manifold. Recall from chapter 5 that natural data such as photos of pets lies on a low-dimensional manifold inside the huge pixel space, and that a deep net learns a smooth approximation of that manifold from samples. A new input that lies *on* the learned manifold, between known points, can be interpreted by interpolation. An input that moves *off* it, along a direction the training data never varied, is mapped somewhere arbitrary. Hence **known unknowns**: you don't know which specific photo will arrive, but you did know (and sample) the kinds of variation it might have. **Data augmentation** (random flips, rotations, zooms in chapter 8) deliberately adds variation along directions you know matter, so the learned manifold extends in those directions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the most practical paragraph in the section. It explains why the best way to improve a deep model is more and better-covering data (p.172), why augmentation is so effective on small datasets (p.276), and why models fail under distribution shift (new camera, new domain, adversarial or unusual inputs). It also sets the ceiling: no amount of interpolation produces the ability to handle **unknown unknowns**, variations nobody anticipated or sampled.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Generalization in deep nets is a coverage problem. If the test point x* is within a small distance of training points along the learned manifold, f(x*) is well constrained by the fit. If not, f(x*) depends on the inductive biases of the architecture and is effectively unconstrained by data.

paragraphs.excerpt: Figure 19.6 Local generalization vs. extreme generalization
paragraphs.what_it_says: The figure has two rows. In each, a 'Situations space' panel on the left shows three known situations as dots, and an arrow leads to a right panel showing the resulting 'Operational area'. Top row: small discs around each dot, labelled 'Lower-intelligence system: lower information conversion ratio'. Bottom row: the same three dots surrounded by a large merged blob, labelled 'Higher-intelligence system: higher information conversion ratio'.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Both systems receive the **same information** (the same three known situations). What differs is the size of the region of situation space where each can act appropriately. The more intelligent system converts the same experience into a much larger operational area, so it generalizes further from what it knows. The small discs are local generalization; the large area moves toward extreme generalization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The figure pictures intelligence as efficiency rather than skill. Because the inputs are held fixed, any difference in output area reflects how well the system turns information into capability. p.604 makes this a definition: intelligence as the conversion ratio between available information and the future operating area.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The 'operational area' is the set of situations where the system produces appropriate behavior. A rough reading of the conversion ratio: ratio ≈ size of operational area ÷ amount of information (experience plus priors) used. The book gives this only informally; the ratio is not given as a formula here.

terminology.meaning: The abstract space of all situations a system might face.
The region of situations space in which the system can produce appropriate behavior.
How much operational area a system obtains per unit of information (experience, priors) it has; the author's efficiency measure of intelligence, developed on p.604.

connections: p.604: intelligence 'can be precisely quantified as an efficiency ratio' between information and future operating area.

paragraphs.excerpt: Consider, for instance, the problem of learning the appropriate launch parameters to get
paragraphs.what_it_says: To learn launch parameters that land a rocket on the moon with supervised or reinforcement learning, a deep net would need tens of thousands or millions of launch trials, a dense sampling of the input space, to learn a reliable input-to-output mapping. Humans use abstraction to build physical models (rocket science) and derive an exact solution that works in one or a few trials. Similarly, a deep net controlling a human body that must learn to navigate a city safely would have to die many thousands of times before inferring that cars are dangerous, and would have to relearn most of it in a new city. (Continued on p.599: humans learn safe behavior without dying even once, thanks to abstract modeling of novel situations.)
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two examples contrast **two sources of generalization**. A deep net generalizes by *covering* the input space with examples and interpolating between them, so its data requirement grows with how much of the space must be covered. A human generalizes by *modeling*: Newtonian mechanics and orbital equations are compact abstractions that are valid for every launch configuration, including ones never tried. The model replaces the data. The city example adds **transfer**: an abstraction such as 'cars are heavy, fast and dangerous' carries over to any city, while a mapping learned from one city's specifics does not.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These examples make Figure 19.6 concrete. They also point to why deep reinforcement learning is notoriously sample-inefficient and why self-driving and robotics work relies on simulators and hand-built world models (p.600 mentions 'painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world').
paragraphs.technical_idea: Dense sampling: to interpolate reliably, training points must lie close together across the whole region of input space you want to handle. In d dimensions, keeping spacing ε needs about (1/ε)^d samples, which is why coverage-based generalization becomes so data-hungry. A physical model has a fixed, small description that is valid everywhere its assumptions hold.

terminology.meaning: Training data that densely covers the entire input manifold the model must handle, required for reliable interpolation.
Learning a policy from reward signals obtained through trial-and-error interaction with an environment.
An abstract description of the world (e.g. Newton's laws) from which behavior in new configurations can be derived.

concepts.name: Local generalization
concepts.definition: Generalization that holds only for inputs close to the training data; the learned mapping quickly stops making sense as inputs deviate from what the model saw during training.
concepts.intuition: Knowing a city only by the streets you've walked: you can find your way between familiar places, but not in a neighborhood you've never visited.
concepts.technical: Arises because deep nets generalize via interpolation on a learned approximation of the data manifold. Any factor of variation must be represented in the training data (known unknowns) for the manifold to capture it.
concepts.significance: In the author's view it is the ceiling of today's deep learning, and the reason for its data hunger and fragility under distribution shift.
concepts.example: The chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats convnet classifies new photos similar to its training set but cannot be trusted on, for example, cartoon drawings of pets.
concepts.misconception: That local generalization is the same as overfitting. A well-regularized model that generalizes well on its test distribution still generalizes only locally.

concepts.name: Known unknowns
concepts.definition: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data.
concepts.intuition: You don't know which exact photo will arrive, but you know it may come from different angles or lighting, and you included those in training.
concepts.technical: Deep nets can generalize across known unknowns because those directions of variation are covered by the training manifold. Unknown unknowns (unanticipated variation) are not covered and are not handled.
concepts.significance: Separates what deep nets can do (handle sampled variation) from what broad and extreme generalization require (handle unanticipated variation, p.600).
concepts.example: Camera angle and lighting for pet photos, explicitly covered by data or augmentation.
concepts.misconception: That a large enough dataset eventually covers all unknowns. The space of possible novelty is open-ended.

concepts.name: Data augmentation
concepts.definition: Expanding the training set with label-preserving random transformations of existing samples.
concepts.intuition: Showing the model the same cat flipped, rotated and zoomed, so it learns that these changes don't matter.
concepts.technical: On this page, augmentation helps because it extends the learned manifold along factors of variation (known unknowns) the raw data underrepresents, making interpolation possible there.
concepts.significance: It explains, from the generalization theory of this chapter, why a technique from chapter 8 works.
concepts.example: RandomFlip, RandomRotation and RandomZoom layers in the chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model.
concepts.misconception: That augmentation teaches abstract invariance in general. It only covers the specific transformations you chose to apply.

concepts.name: Information conversion ratio
concepts.definition: How efficiently a system converts the information it has (known situations, experience, priors) into an operational area, the set of situations it can handle.
concepts.intuition: Two students read the same three worked examples; the one who can then solve far more new problems has the higher ratio.
concepts.technical: Introduced visually in Figure 19.6 and defined on p.604 as an efficiency ratio between relevant available information and future operating area.
concepts.significance: It is the author's proposed definition of intelligence: efficiency of generalization rather than amount of skill.
concepts.example: A physicist deriving a launch trajectory from equations (high ratio) vs. a deep net needing millions of trials (low ratio).
concepts.misconception: That a system with a bigger operational area is necessarily more intelligent; if it used vastly more data, its ratio may be lower.

deeper.title: Why dense sampling gets expensive
deeper.body:
A back-of-envelope illustration (not in the book) of why 'tens of thousands or even millions of launch trials' is plausible for a coverage-based learner.

Suppose launch parameters have $d$ relevant inputs (angle, thrust profile, timing, mass, ...), each normalized to $[0,1]$, and reliable interpolation needs a training point within spacing $\varepsilon$ along each axis. A grid needs about $(1/\varepsilon)^d$ samples:

- $d=3,\ \varepsilon=0.1$: $10^3 = 1{,}000$ trials
- $d=6,\ \varepsilon=0.1$: $10^6 = 1{,}000{,}000$ trials

Real manifolds are lower-dimensional than the raw input space, which is why deep learning works at all (chapter 5), but the cost still grows quickly with the number of factors of variation. A physical model replaces this table with a few equations valid for every point.

deeper.title: Interpolation vs. extrapolation in one dimension
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a minimal picture of local generalization (see the chart):

1. Sample a smooth function (here $\sin x$) at points in $[-3, 3]$ and fit a flexible model (a degree-7 polynomial).
2. Inside $[-3,3]$ the fit tracks the truth closely: the model generalizes to new $x$ *between* training points.
3. Just outside, at $x=\pm 3.5$, it starts to drift. By $x=4.5$ it predicts values far outside $[-1,1]$, values the true function never takes.

Nothing in the training data constrained the model out there, so its behavior is decided by the model family, not the data. A deep net on a manifold behaves the same way, except that 'outside' means off the learned manifold, along variation directions never sampled.

deeper.title: Abstraction as compression of the solution
deeper.body: The rocket example can be read as a contrast between storing **answers** and storing a **generator of answers**. A deep net effectively stores a smooth lookup surface from launch conditions to parameters, and needs many points to pin it down. Rocket science stores the generator: $F = ma$, gravitation, and the rocket equation. From them, the answer for any configuration is derived on demand. This is the 'modular, reusable abstractions that can be quickly repurposed' that p.599 credits to understanding.

visualizations.title: Local generalization: good inside the training range, meaningless outside
visualizations.why: Illustrates the page's claim that a learned mapping 'quickly stops making sense as inputs start deviating from what the net saw at training time'. A flexible model fit on x ∈ [−3, 3] tracks sin(x) there and diverges beyond (values clipped at ±3). AI-made illustration, not from the book.

misconceptions.claim: If a model generalizes well to its held-out test set, it will generalize to new real-world situations.
misconceptions.correction: A test set drawn from the training distribution only measures local generalization to known unknowns. Inputs that deviate along unsampled factors of variation can break the mapping.

misconceptions.claim: Data augmentation makes a model robust to novelty in general.
misconceptions.correction: It extends coverage only along the specific transformations applied (flips, rotations, lighting). It is a way of adding known unknowns, not a source of improvisation.

misconceptions.claim: Figure 19.6 shows that more intelligent systems need more known situations.
misconceptions.correction: Both rows use the same three known situations. The higher-intelligence system turns the same information into a larger operational area, which is the point of the 'information conversion ratio' labels.

misconceptions.claim: Reinforcement learning avoids the dense-sampling problem because it learns from interaction.
misconceptions.correction: The author names both supervised and reinforcement learning: either way a deep net needs a dense sampling of the input space, for RL in the form of a huge number of trials.

takeaways: Deep nets handle inputs that deviate a bit from the training data, which is what makes them useful, but only locally.
Local generalization: the learned mapping quickly stops making sense as inputs move away from what was seen in training.
Deep nets generalize only to known unknowns, factors of variation anticipated and well represented in training data.
The cause is interpolation on a learned manifold (chapter 5); this is also why data augmentation helps.
Figure 19.6: from the same known situations, a more intelligent system gets a larger operational area (higher information conversion ratio).
Deep nets need dense sampling (millions of rocket launches, thousands of deaths in traffic); humans use abstract models to succeed in one or a few trials.

questions.question: What does the author mean by 'known unknowns', and give the page's example?
questions.answer: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data, such as different camera angles or lighting conditions for pet pictures.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in e03. Deep nets can only generalize across such anticipated, well-sampled variation.

questions.question: According to the page, why is basic data augmentation so helpful for deep net generalization?
options: It reduces the number of parameters the model needs
Deep nets generalize via interpolation on a manifold, so every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold, and augmentation supplies such variation
It lets the model build abstract physical models of the input
It replaces the need for a validation set
questions.answer: Deep nets generalize via interpolation on a manifold, so every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold, and augmentation supplies such variation
questions.explanation: The text links the two directly: 'any factor of variation in their input space needs to be captured by the manifold they learn. That's why basic data augmentation is so helpful.' Augmentation does not change parameter count, does not produce abstract models (the thing deep nets lack), and does not replace validation.

questions.question: In Figure 19.6, both rows start from the same three known situations. Why is that design choice essential to the figure's message?
questions.answer: Because it holds the information fixed. The only difference is how large an operational area each system obtains from that information, so the figure illustrates intelligence as efficiency (information conversion ratio), not as amount of experience or skill.
questions.explanation: The labels 'lower/higher information conversion ratio' and the identical dot configurations show this; p.604 formalizes it as an efficiency ratio.

questions.question: Contrast how a deep net and a human would solve the rocket-landing problem, and explain where each one's generalization comes from.
questions.answer: The deep net needs tens of thousands to millions of trials (a dense sampling of input space) and generalizes by interpolating between them. The human uses abstraction to build a physical model (rocket science) and derives an exact solution in one or a few trials. The model's validity across all configurations is what provides generalization.
questions.explanation: This is the page's e05 example. It contrasts coverage-based generalization (interpolation) with model-based generalization (abstraction).

questions.question: In the city-navigation example, what happens when the deep net is dropped into a new city?
options: It would have to relearn most of what it knows
questions.answer: It would have to relearn most of what it knows
questions.explanation: The text says: 'Dropped into a new city, the net would have to relearn most of what it knows.' The learned mapping is tied to the specifics of the training city rather than an abstraction like 'cars are dangerous'. The other options contradict the page.

questions.question: Which earlier model does the author use as an example of useful local generalization, and what condition limits it?
questions.answer: The dogs-vs-cats model from chapter 8. It classifies unseen cat or dog pictures only as long as they are close enough to what it was trained on.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of e03.

questions.question: Pick a model you have deployed or trained. List two factors of variation you covered (known unknowns) and one plausible unknown unknown that could break it.
questions.answer: Open answer. Example for a pet classifier: known unknowns are lighting and pose (covered by data and augmentation); an unknown unknown is pets in costumes or a thermal camera image.
questions.explanation: Applying the known/unknown-unknown distinction to real systems is how this page's theory becomes practical robustness thinking.
